sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Platinum-resistant high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas (HGSOC) are associated with poor therapeutic outcomes. Although HGSOC frequently metastasizes to the intraperitoneal (IP) cavity, the success of IP cytokine therapies, such as IL2, has been hampered by local toxicity and administration difficulties. AVB-001 is a novel IL2 delivery system consisting of encapsulated, allogeneic cells engineered for constitutive human IL2 (hIL2) expression.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: This is a phase I dose-escalation trial of AVB-001 for the treatment of HGSOC (NCT05538624). A single dose of AVB-001 was administered by IP laparoscopy, enabling hIL2 doses from 0.6 to 3.6 μg hIL2/kg/day. Safety was evaluated using NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v5.0. Efficacy was assessed via Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) v1.1 and immunotherapy RECIST criteria.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: The trial enrolled 14 patients across four dose levels. Three (21.4%) patients experienced grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAE); no grade 4 to 5 TRAEs were reported. There was one dose-limiting toxicity. There was one unconfirmed partial response but no confirmed responses (overall response rate 0%). Stable disease was observed in seven patients, with a median duration of 2.57 months (range, 2.03–4.23). The clinical benefit rate was 14.3% (n = 2). Pharmacokinetics demonstrated dose-dependent increases in serum IL2, peaking at 1 day after implantation. Immunologic analyses revealed sustained CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell proliferation without corresponding proliferation in regulatory T cells. Dose-dependent CTLA-4 receptor upregulation was observed on CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, whereas PD-1 and TIM-3 remained unchanged.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: In patients with HGSOC, AVB-001 is safe and effectively activates cytotoxic T cells, supporting further investigation of this locoregional immunotherapy.

boxed-text.p: In this phase I dose-escalation trial, we demonstrate the clinical activity of a novel drug (AVB-001) delivered intraperitoneally for the treatment of platinum-resistant high-grade serous ovarian cancer. In a prior publication, we demonstrated the preclinical efficacy of IL2-secreting encapsulated cell therapies in mouse models. This study advances the concept into the clinic and describes the first-in-human use of living IL2 factories designed for localized intraperitoneal immunotherapy in patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. This encapsulated cell technology permits sustained and self-limited delivery of local cytokine therapy, a treatment option that has previously had limited use due to challenges with administration and toxicity. This trial provides support for the safety, feasibility, and preliminary immunologic activity of this approach and offers a compelling step toward a new modality of immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cancers originating from the ovary, fallopian tube, or peritoneum account for more than 20,000 new cancer cases annually in the United States and more than 12,000 deaths per year (1). Of these, the majority are of high-grade serous histology, hereafter collectively referred to as high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas (HGSOC), which are often diagnosed at an advanced stage and are characterized by an aggressive natural history and a high rate of recurrence (2). Although approximately 70% to 80% of patients respond to first-line treatment with platinum-doublet chemotherapy and surgical cytoreduction, the majority ultimately experience recurrence (3, 4). In the recurrent setting, the disease becomes incurable, and response rates decline with subsequent lines of therapy, resulting in the inevitable development of platinum-resistant disease with an associated median overall survival (OS) of approximately 12 months (5).

A common feature of HGSOC is its propensity to metastasize throughout the peritoneal cavity (6). This behavior has generated particular interest in the development of efficacious locoregional treatments administered via an intraperitoneal (IP) route (7–9). The IP route of administration is intriguing because it permits a several-fold increase in drug concentration within the abdominal cavity and less systemic toxicity compared with the intravenous route (10–13). For patients with advanced-stage surgically debulked ovarian cancer, IP chemotherapy has previously been associated with a potential survival advantage (14, 15). Widespread adaptation, however, has not occurred due to administration difficulties and the potential for local toxicity (16, 17).

Immunotherapy has previously demonstrated promise as a strategy for treating ovarian cancer. In particular, intravenous administration of interleukin 2 (IL2), a cytokine known for its ability to activate and expand cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, has demonstrated significant activity in the treatment of melanoma and renal cell carcinoma (18, 19). However, its short serum half-life has required it to be administered in high doses with an elevated risk of severe inflammatory toxicities (20, 21). To mitigate these side effects, researchers have investigated localized IP delivery of IL2. In a pivotal study, Edwards and colleagues (22) reported an overall response rate (ORR) of 25.7% in patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer receiving IP IL2. A subsequent trial yielded comparable results, with an ORR of 25%; however, 45% of patients were unable to complete treatment due to adverse events (AE), primarily catheter-associated complications (23). Although these studies underscore the therapeutic potential of locally delivered IL2, they also highlight the urgent need for safer, more effective delivery strategies.

This challenge led to the development of an encapsulated, bioengineered, retinal pigmented epithelial cell therapy platform that enables localized, continuous secretion of biologic agents, including IL2. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that these IL2 encapsulated protein producers (ePP) achieve sustained, high, local cytokine concentrations with minimal systemic distribution in both murine and nonhuman primates (13, 24). In murine models of ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, and malignant pleural mesothelioma, IL2 cytokine factories induced robust activation and proliferation of cytotoxic T cells within the tumor microenvironment, leading to complete tumor regression and the establishment of durable immunologic memory upon rechallenge (13, 24).

This study describes the first-in-human administration of localized IL2-producing ePPs (termed AVB-001) to the IP space in patients with platinum-resistant HGSOC. The primary objectives were to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and tolerability of AVB-001 after a single IP administration and to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Translational objectives were to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK) and immunologic pharmacodynamics of AVB-001.

sec.title: Alginate preparation and capsule production
sec.p: GMP-grade SLG20 sodium alginate was hydrated with sterile 0.9% saline at a concentration of 1.4% w/v and mixed overnight under agitation. The alginate was then filtered through a 0.2-μm PES filter and aseptically aliquoted. Aliquots were stored at 2°C to 8°C until use. Capsules were produced as described previously (7, 24). Briefly, cells were suspended in alginate warmed to room temperature at a concentration of 40e6 viable cells/mL. The cell–alginate suspension was extruded by syringe pump at 5 mL/hour through the inner 22G lumen of a coaxial needle. Hydrated alginate was simultaneously extruded through the outer 18G lumen of the coaxial needle at 5 mL/hour. The coaxial needle was connected to a DC power supply, allowing capsules to form and collect in a bath of 20 mmol/L barium chloride solution. During manufacturing, the drop rate was periodically monitored to ensure that capsules maintained a consistent size. Voltage was increased when the drop rate was measured as less than 9 drops per 10 seconds. Voltage was decreased when the drop rate was measured as above 11 drops per 10 seconds. Once all materials had been extruded, capsules were allowed to cross-link for an additional 5 to 7 minutes, after which they were transferred to a PETG bottle. Capsules were washed for 2 minutes in 200 mL of phenol-free DMEM/F12 on a tube rotor set to 40 RPM. Eight washings were performed, after which capsules were stored in fresh DMEM/F12. When sufficient material had been manufactured, capsules were pooled together. Capsules were formulated into 1 or 5 mL dosing aliquots in phenol-free DMEM/F12 at a ratio of 1 mL of capsules to 100 mL of media. Aliquots for dosing were stored at room temperature in a controlled environment until administration.

sec.title: Capsule cell viability
sec.p: In triplicate, 10 capsules were incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes in 200 μL of DMEM/F12 supplemented to contain 1 mg/mL alginate lyase, 10% v/v fetal bovine serum (FBS; Cytiva), and 5 mmol/L EDTA. Following incubation, capsules were mechanically disrupted by gentle pipetting. For research cell counts and viability, cell suspensions were mixed 1:1 with Trypan Blue and added to microfluid cell counting slides. Slides were immediately analyzed on a Countess (Thermo Fisher Scientific) automated cell counter to quantify cell concentration and viability. Clinical samples were instead added to a Via1-Cassette (Chemometec) and analyzed on an NC-200.

sec.title: Quantification of human IL2 production in capsules
sec.p: In triplicate, five capsules were plated in a single well of a 48-well plate and incubated in DMEM/F12 culture media supplemented to 10% v/v FBS media for 4 to 24 hours. The supernatant was collected and frozen at −20°C. Samples were analyzed for human IL2 (hIL2) concentration using the Human IL2 Quantikine ELISA Kit (R&D Systems).

sec.title: Mycoplasma testing—drug product
sec.p: A sample of formulated drug product storage solution was collected. Sample submitted to an external vendor (IDEXX BioAnalytics) for Mycoplasma testing via real-time PCR.

sec.title: Mycoplasma testing—drug substance
sec.p: Approximately 5e5 to 1e6 cells were aliquoted in a tube and frozen at −80°C. The sample was submitted to an external vendor (IDEXX BioAnalytics) for Mycoplasma testing via real-time PCR.

sec.title: Sterility testing
sec.p: A sample of formulated drug product storage solution was collected and submitted to an external vendor (IDEXX BioAnalytics). The sample was inoculated into growth media and observed for signs of contamination. For clinical drug product, samples were prepared similarly and submitted to Eurofins. The sample was tested according to USP <71> standards. Samples were similarly collected for rapid sterility testing used for the generation of a Certificate of Testing. Samples from the drug product were collected, inoculated into BACT/ALERT media vials, and sent to an external vendor (Eurofins) for growth monitoring.

sec.title: Endotoxin testing
sec.p: The storage solution of formulated test and control article was collected and submitted to Associates of Cape Cod or Focus Labs for research and clinical samples, respectively. Samples were assessed for kinetic-chromogenic endotoxin detection. The limit of detection for clinical samples was <0.05 EU/mL.

sec.title: Residual barium testing
sec.p: Residual barium concentration was measured to ensure that the barium level in the drug product was below the threshold for toxicity. The storage solution of formulated test and control article was collected and submitted to an external vendor (Intertek or Eurofins for research and clinical samples, respectively) for ion chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis. For clinical samples, the limit of detection was 6.25 ppm.

sec.title: Capsule fracture strength
sec.p: Capsule fracture strength was measured to ensure that the drug product had sufficient material mechanical integrity for handling and administration. Twenty individual capsules were analyzed for initial fracture using a TA-XT.Plus texture analyzer (TA Instruments). Capsules were compressed to 90% strain, from which the applied force at the initial fracture force was determined.

sec.title: Residual bovine serum albumin testing
sec.p: Residual bovine serum albumin (BSA) was measured as a marker for bovine serum used in the manufacturing process. Residual BSA and other serum components may cause immune responses ranging from mild to severe. A sample of drug product storage solution was collected in low–protein-binding microcentrifuge tubes. Samples were run on a BSA ELISA kit (Cygnus Technologies).

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This was an open-label, multicenter, phase I dose-escalation study of AVB-001 in patients with platinum-resistant or refractory, high-grade serous adenocarcinoma of the ovary, primary peritoneum, or fallopian tube (NCT05538624). The study consisted of a single-dose administration of AVB-001 at one of four dose levels. The dose of the capsules was based on the projected amount of hIL2 produced by the capsules on a per-kilogram and per-day basis. The starting dose was 0.6 μg hIL2/kg/day. To determine the starting dose, data on dosing were extrapolated from preclinical studies in nonhuman primates (NHP) to ensure that the selected starting dose would keep blood levels below 5,590 pg/mL (22). The maximum dose was capped at 3.6 μg hIL2/kg/day.

The primary objectives were to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and tolerability of AVB-001 after a single IP administration and to determine the MTD and the RP2D. Secondary objectives included translational correlates to assess the PK and immunologic response in the peripheral blood, preliminary efficacy evaluation using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) v1.1, and preliminary efficacy evaluation per the modified RECIST guideline for immunotherapy (iRECIST).

Participants in the study were required to have histologically confirmed, metastatic or unresectable, platinum-resistant or platinum-refractory, high-grade serous adenocarcinoma. Platinum-resistance was defined as either relapse within 6 months of initial platinum-containing chemotherapy or, if previously platinum-sensitive, progression after receiving at least two lines of platinum-containing chemotherapy. Platinum-refractory was defined as progression during the initial exposure to platinum-based chemotherapy. Participants must have received a maximum of five lines of prior therapy, have an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score of 0 to 1, and have adequate renal, hepatic, and hematologic functions. Because of the route of administration, all patients were required to have IP disease with evidence of measurable disease as defined by RECIST v1.1 on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Key exclusion criteria included those with nonserous or mixed histologies, individuals with a synchronous primary or prior malignancy within 3 years, presence of clinical signs or symptoms concerning for partial or complete gastrointestinal obstruction or fistula, history of gastrointestinal bleeding within the past 6 months, history of an autoimmune or inflammatory disease excluding endocrine autoimmune disease treated with hormone replacement, use of chronic immunosuppressive therapy, prior administration of IL2 or IL2-like molecules, or any prior IP gene-targeted therapy.

A Bayesian optimal interval design was used to identify the MTD/RP2D. Patients were enrolled and treated in cohorts of 3. The first cohort of three patients was staggered to minimize potential risks associated with the first-in-human administration of AVB-001. Escalation to the next higher dose level was based on the targeted toxicity rate of approximately 30% for the MTD. The decision to escalate or deescalate was based on whether the observed probability of a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) at the current dose is ≤0.236 or ≥0.359, respectively. If the probability of a DLT is at or below 0.236, dose-escalation to the next higher dose occurred. If the probability of a DLT is >0.236 and <0.359, the dose was maintained for the next three patients. A safety review committee was established to review and determine escalation and deescalation decisions, AEs, and DLTs. The trial was initially designed to include a phase II dose expansion phase; however, the study was ultimately terminated after the dose-escalation phase because of funding limitations.

DLTs were evaluated over a 4-week period following study drug administration. Grading of DLTs followed National Cancer Institute (NCI) Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0 guidelines. Hematologic DLTs were defined as grade 4 neutropenia lasting more than 7 days, febrile neutropenia, grade 4 anemia not resolving in 7 days, grade 4 thrombocytopenia, or grade 3 thrombocytopenia lasting more than 7 days or associated with significant bleeding. Nonhematologic DLTs were defined as grade 3 or higher toxicities probably or possibly related to any study procedures, grade 3 or higher toxicities involving major organs systems that are not preexisting or related to underlying malignancy, grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome, hypotension event, or allergic reaction at least possibly related to the study drug that does not resolve to grade 1 or less within 72 hours, grade 2 or higher neurotoxicity that does not resolve to grade 1 or lower within 72 hours, aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase (AST/ALT) elevation at least three times the upper limit of normal with concurrent increase in bilirubin to two times the upper limit of normal, AST/ALT elevation over eight times the upper limit of normal irrespective of bilirubin level, or total bilirubin over five times the upper limit of normal irrespective of AST/ALT elevation level. For additional details regarding DLT definitions and exclusions, please refer to the protocol provided in the Supplementary Materials.

This study involves human participants and was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and the Institutional Review Boards at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (protocol #2022-0420), Massachusetts General Hospital, the Center for Cancer Research at the NCI, and Women and Infants Hospital. All participants provided written informed consent, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Council for Harmonisation guidelines for Good Clinical Practice.

sec.title: Drug administration
sec.p: Participants underwent a minimally invasive laparoscopic procedure to permit administration of the study drug into the IP cavity. Routine anesthesia and cardiovascular monitoring were performed throughout the procedure. Following laparoscopic entry and visual assessment of the peritoneal cavity by standard techniques, a second incision was made, and a trocar was introduced. An Argyle Tenckhoff peritoneal catheter was then inserted through this trocar. The catheter was inserted in accordance with standard-of-care considerations; however, preferred administration sites, when feasible, included the infracolic omental remnant, supracolic omentum, or paracolic gutters. Care was taken to minimize bleeding throughout the procedure due to the risk of shortening the lifespan of the cells when in contact with blood as a result of accelerated pericapsular overgrowth.

Following placement, the outer cannula of the catheter was then connected in a sterile fashion to a sterile syringe loaded with a fixed ratio of capsules and saline at a volume of 40 mL per syringe. The syringe contents were then dispensed through the catheter into the IP cavity using a slow bolus push at a rate of approximately 1 to 2 minutes per syringe. Additional syringes were utilized for escalating dose levels. After all capsules had been administered, an additional 10 mL of saline was used to flush the catheter of any remaining drug product. The catheter was removed, and the procedure was concluded. Postoperatively, the first three patients treated with the study drug were admitted for at least 24 hours of observation to monitor for the occurrence of AEs related to the procedure and drug administration. After the initial three-patient cohort, postoperative discharge readiness was per institutional standard of care. Additional information about capsule preparation and delivery can be viewed in the supplemental cell therapy preparation and administration manual.

sec.title: Study assessments
sec.p: Patients were evaluable for response if they had received the full dose of the study drug and undergone at least one postbaseline efficacy assessment. Response to treatment within the study cohort was assessed with serial imaging via CT or MRI. Imaging assessment was conducted at screening and at posttreatment assessment intervals. Serial imaging was continued until progressive disease (PD) by RECIST v1.1 was noted. At the time of the initial PD assessment, patients were permitted to remain on study without initiating other anticancer therapies until an additional confirmatory assessment was conducted at 4 weeks from the initial scan documenting progression due to the potential for pseudoprogression with response to immunotherapy. Per iRECIST v1.1, if confirmed PD (iCPD) was noted at the follow-up scan, then the patient was withdrawn from the study.

AE assessment was conducted continuously from the time of the administration of the study drug and included those related to either surgery or drug. The nature, incidence, relatedness, and severity of all AEs, including the occurrence of any DLTs, were reported according to the NCI CTCAE v5.0. All patients exposed to AVB-001 were evaluated for safety.

To assess pharmacodynamics and determine the potential for AVB-001 to induce immunogenicity, peripheral blood samples were collected at baseline and specified posttreatment time points. Sampling was standardized across dose levels and patients according to the schedule of activities.

sec.title: Flow cytometry sample preparation and staining
sec.p: Aliquots of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and IP fluid samples were stored in liquid nitrogen for retrospective analysis. Upon thawing, samples underwent cell count and cell viability quality control (QC) checks on a Cellometer K2 Cell Counter (Nexcelom Bioscience). Samples with no viable cells were excluded from analysis. PBMCs were spun down, washed, and resuspended in FACS wash buffer (1× DPBS with 1% BSA). Flow cytometry staining was performed for myeloid (Supplementary Table S1) and functional and memory T cells (Supplementary Table S2), respectively.

Following staining, acquisition was performed on a LSRFortessa TM X-20 (Becton Dickinson) flow cytometer using FACSDiva software (FACSDiva, RRID: SCR_001456). Samples failing to meet the QC metric of >100 CD45+ live-cell events were excluded from analysis. The acquired data were subsequently processed using FlowJo v10 software (FlowJo, RRID: SCR_008520).

sec.title: Myeloid panel gating
sec.p: Lymphocytes were identified based on size and granularity using a forward scatter area (FSC-A) versus side scatter area (SSC-A) plot. Next, single cells were identified by excluding doublets using FSC-height (FSC-H) versus FSC-A and sequential SSC-height (SSC-H) versus SSC-A plots. A time gate was applied to ensure consistent flow and eliminate irregularities. Live cells were then identified using viability dye. CD45-positive events, representing leukocytes, were selected using an FSC versus CD45 plot. A dump gate was applied to remove unwanted cells by gating HLA-DR expression versus dump gate which excluded CD3/CD19/CD20/CD55-positive cells. Monocytes and dendritic cells (DC) were gated by the expression of HLA-DR versus CD14. HLA-DR is a marker of antigen-presenting cells, and CD14 is a monocyte marker. From the HLA-DR+ CD14+ population, cells were further gated on CD16 versus CD14 expression. CD14+ cells were classified into three monocyte subsets based on CD16 expression: classic monocytes (CD14+ CD16−), intermediate monocytes (CD14+ CD16+), and nonclassic monocytes (CD14dim CD16+). The HLA-DR− CD14+ population was further gated by CD33 expression. From the HLA-DR+ CD14−population, CD11b versus CD11c gating was used to distinguish activated monocytes and DCs (CD11b− CD11c+). Further gating of the CD11b+ CD11c+ population by CD141 expression versus CD1c expression was performed to identify DC1 (CD141+) and DC3 (CD141−) subsets. The CD11b+ CD11c−population was further gated by CD123 used to identify plasmacytoid DCs (pDC).

sec.title: Functional and memory T-cell gating
sec.p: Lymphocytes were identified based on size and granularity using a FSC-A versus SSC-A plot. Single cells were identified by gating for FSC-H versus FSC-A and sequential SSC-H versus SSC-A. A time gate was applied to ensure consistent flow and eliminate irregularities. Live cells were then identified using viability dye. CD45-positive events, representing leukocytes, were selected using an FSC versus CD45 plot. The CD45+ population was then gated by CD3 expression to select T cells, which were subsequently gated by CD4+ and CD8+ populations. Memory subsets were defined based on CCR7 and CD45RA expression, distinguishing naïve (CCR7+CD45RA+), central memory (CCR7+CD45RA−), effector memory (CCR7−CD45RA−), and terminal effector (CCR7−CD45RA+) cells. Effector memory cells were classified into four subsets based on CD27 and CD28 expression: EM1 (CD27+ and CD29+), EM2 (CD27+ and CD28−, seen only in the CD8+ population), EM2 (CD27− and CD28−), and EM4 (CD27− and CD28+). EM2 was only seen in the CD8+ population. Functional analysis follows, with markers such as ICOS, CD25, CD28, and Ki67 identifying activation and proliferation states, whereas PD-1, Tim-3, and CTLA-4 assess exhaustion. FoxP3 versus CD25 gating was used to identify regulatory T cells (Treg) from the CD4+ population.

sec.title: Clinical serum analysis
sec.p: Serum cytokine concentrations were measured by Medpace Reference Laboratories. Serum IL2 levels were measured by Medpace Bioanalytical Laboratories via electrochemiluminescence assay. All samples were processed, shipped, and stored in accordance with the laboratory’s specified requirements.

sec.title: Mathematical modeling of AVB-001 PK
sec.p: A mathematical model of AVB-001 PK was developed based on a previously published model of the system (MATLAB, RRID: SCR_001622; ref. 13). Model parameters were estimated with nonlinear mixed effects modeling with proportional error using the nlmixr package in R with the SAEM parameter estimation method (25, 26). Initial parameter estimates were obtained by estimating individual patient parameter sets with the naïve pooled approach, and all parameters were assumed to be log-normally distributed. Fixed- and random-effect parameters were determined by first assuming all parameters are random effects and then removing random effects on all parameters with a shrinkage value greater than 30%. The final version of the model was then used to estimate the amount of AVB-001–produced IL2 in the peritoneal cavity throughout the course of treatment.

sec.title: Animal model and study design
sec.p: Four Mauritian cynomolgus macaques, adult females (10–15 years old, 2–8 kg) and adult males (5–7 years old, 3–9 kg), were used in this study. All macaque study subjects were naïve to prior procedures. Each subject was assigned a unique 4-digit numerical identifier (CN9171, CN9313, CN9317, and CN9314). They were housed with ad libitum access to food and water under standard light/dark cycles. Cage checks were conducted throughout the study to monitor the behavior and overall health of the animals. All studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

Capsule delivery was performed under standard sterile precautions in a surgical suite. The anterior abdomen was shaved and prepped from the xiphoid process to the pubis. A small (2 cm) supraumbilical incision was made, and a 5- to 12-mm trocar was inserted. Pneumoperitoneum was created using CO2 at a pressure of 10 to 14 mm Hg. The peritoneal cavity was warmed with heated saline, and a laparoscopic camera was introduced through the trocar to provide visualization. Under laparoscopic guidance, a second small incision (1 cm) was made, and a 5- to 12-mm trocar was inserted. Capsules were delivered into the peritoneal cavity using an Argyle Tenckhoff peritoneal catheter (Ref 8810889003) connected to a 60 mL sterile Luer lock syringe. Capsules were suspended in sterile saline at a ratio of approximately 7 mL of saline per mL of capsule, with no more than 5 mL of capsule delivered per syringe. Each primate received a dose of approximately 10 μg/kg/day AVB-001 hIL2. Control primates received saline only, with volume calculated based on weight. Laparoscopic videos and images were recorded to confirm the absence of abnormalities within the peritoneal cavity. Upon completion of the procedure, the small incisions were closed in layers using Vicryl 3-0 for muscle and a 4-0 subcuticular suture for the skin.

Animals were monitored throughout the study for behavioral or health abnormalities. Clinical observations for signs such as labored breathing, facial redness, vomiting, tremors, lethargy, or diarrhea were conducted three times weekly, with abnormal findings documented. Body weight and rectal temperature were measured throughout the study. Blood samples were collected via intravenous draws for hematologic, clinical chemistry, and coagulation analyses.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive summary statistics were used to describe demographics and clinical characteristics of the evaluable patients. Flow cytometry data were normalized using the range function in JMP Pro 15 (Min–Max approach), adjusting values to a range of 0 to 1. Normalization was performed separately for each set of surface checkpoint inhibitor markers. The data were then transformed to visualize fold differences relative to the mean of the baseline points for each checkpoint inhibitor. The peak value from each patient was selected. All data were analyzed and visualized using GraphPad Prism (version 10.2.2, GraphPad Software, RRID: SCR_002798). Statistical significance was assessed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A family-wise α threshold of 0.05 was applied, corresponding to a 95% confidence interval (CI). Data are presented as the mean ± SEM, and statistical significance is denoted in the figure where applicable.

sec.title: Clinical-grade (GMP) manufacturing of AVB-001 for human testing
sec.p: AVB-001 is an encapsulated cell product consisting of allogeneic, genetically enhanced retinal pigment epithelial cells engineered to secrete hIL2 (retinal pigment epithelial cell line, RRID: CVCL_0145). The manufacturing process follows a standardized workflow involving cell expansion, batch harvesting, and encapsulation via electrostatic spraying, a technique validated across multiple preclinical models, including murine and nonhuman primate studies (13, 24). Cell expansion occurs over 28 days, yielding approximately 1.2 billion cells before sequential harvesting and encapsulation (D29; Supplementary Fig. S1). Encapsulation is achieved using a syringe pump–driven electrostatic spraying system, where alginate-embedded cells are formed into uniform capsules with a controlled diameter of 1.5 mm. Following encapsulation, pooled batches undergo stringent QC assessments, with each batch formulated and stored for up to 10 days prior to preparation for clinical administration.

To ensure clinical-grade reproducibility, rigorous manufacturing criteria were evaluated across all production runs, demonstrating consistent adherence to predefined specifications (Supplementary Table S4). Key drug substance attributes, including cell viability (>90%, measured at 96% ± 1%) and IL2 secretion (>0.5 pg/cell/day, measured at 0.8 ± 0.2 pg/cell/day), met or exceeded acceptance criteria. Drug product assessments confirmed stable pH (7.19 ± 0.06), osmolality (302 ± 2 mOsm/kg), and capsule morphology (>70% conforming, achieved at 97% ± 5%). Furthermore, each batch was evaluated for sterility, endotoxin levels, and residual FBS, with all tested samples meeting predefined safety thresholds. Notably, the encapsulated product exhibited robust fracture strength (>15 g, measured at 18.9 ± 1.9 g), ensuring mechanical stability throughout handling and administration (Supplementary Table S4). The consistency of these results underscores the robustness and reproducibility of AVB-001 manufacturing, supporting its clinical translation and scalable production for future studies.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: The trial enrolled 14 patients between November 2022 and November 2023. Eleven patients had primary ovarian cancer (78.6%), two had primary fallopian tube cancer (14.2%), and one had primary peritoneal cancer (7.1%). All patients were evaluable for efficacy and safety. Clinical and demographic information for the study population is depicted in Table 1. Notably, five patients had previously received immunotherapy (35.7%), 11 had previously received bevacizumab (78.6%), and the median number of prior lines of therapy was 2 (range, 1–4). Three patients received dose level 1 (6–9 mL AVB-001), three received dose level 2 (14–17 mL AVB-001), five received dose level 3 (22–34 mL AVB-001), and three received dose level 4 (31–50 mL AVB-001), respectively.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: There were 11 (78.6%) patients who experienced any treatment-related AE (TRAE). The most common events were anemia, chills, eosinophilia, fatigue, fever, and rash, as shown in Table 2. There were no grade 4 or 5 TRAEs. Three (21.4%) patients experienced a grade 3 TRAE. One patient experienced bowel perforation, two episodes of anemia, and fatigue. The other two patients experienced nausea and rash, respectively. The MTD and RP2D for AVB-001 were not reached.

sec.p: There was one DLT that occurred at dose level 3 in the setting of bowel perforation. On study day 1, the participant underwent uncomplicated laparoscopy-assisted administration of AVB-001, which was notable for diffuse peritoneal carcinomatosis. The patient subsequently presented to the hospital in distributive shock on study day 8. Imaging at that time was notable for wall thickening throughout the small and large bowels, as well as a small amount of nondependent gas. By study day 12, the patient had clinically improved with antibiotics and intravenous fluids. Imaging was subsequently repeated on study day 14 because of clinical worsening and observation of pneumoperitoneum. The patient was taken to the operating room, where a microperforation of the bowel was noted and repaired. The operative findings were additionally notable for resolution of previously noted carcinomatosis, diffuse peritoneal inflammation, and no evidence of tumor at or around the perforation site. The event was reviewed by the safety review committee and attributed to the treatment. Dose level 3 was expanded without further events; therefore, dose-escalation was permitted. No other participants in the study experienced bowel perforation.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: All treated patients were included in the efficacy analysis. Objective tumor response, assessed according to RECIST v1.1 and iRECIST, demonstrated an ORR of 0%. One patient demonstrated an initial unconfirmed partial response; however, confirmatory assessment revealed PD. Seven (50%) patients experienced stable disease (SD), with a median duration of clinical stability lasting 2.57 months (range, 2.03–4.23; Fig. 1A). From this group, two individuals had a duration of clinical stability greater than 4 months, resulting in a clinical benefit rate (CBR) of 14.3%. A dose-dependent trend in disease stabilization was observed, with the highest dose cohort (3.6 μg hIL2/kg/day) exhibiting the longest mean duration of disease control. The percentage change from baseline in the target lesion size for each patient is illustrated in Fig. 1B. The best response as a percentage change from baseline tumor volume is shown in Supplementary Fig. S2.

sec.title: Observed PK
sec.p: The level of IL2 was assessed via serial plasma concentration measurements at baseline and at 12, 24, 72, 168, 336, 504, and 648 hours following AVB-001 administration. Plasma IL2 levels peaked at 24 hours (1 day) after administration, which was followed by a steady decline in concentration and a return to baseline levels by 336 hours (7 days) after administration (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Fig. S3). Peak serum IL2 concentrations increased linearly with respect to dose (R2 = 0.7413; Supplementary Fig. S4). To estimate the levels of IL2 in the peritoneal cavity following AVB-001 administration, a two-compartment mathematical model was developed, and individual patient parameters were estimated using nonlinear effects modeling (Fig. 2B; Supplementary Figs. S4 and S5; Supplementary Tables S5–S9; Supplementary Text). Model fits were in good agreement with measured serum IL2 concentrations (Fig. 2C–F), and modeled predictions of IL2 in the peritoneal cavity were comparable with the amounts administered in a phase I clinical trial of peritoneal infusions of recombinant IL2 (Fig. 2G–J; ref. 22). IP concentrations could not be predicted with high confidence due to the uncertainty of peritoneal fluid volumes. However, concentrations estimated based on varying peritoneal volumes reveal that even in cases of significant IP fluid accumulation, IL2 concentrations are at least 7× higher in the peritoneal cavity compared with blood (Supplementary Table S8). Furthermore, our results illustrate that patient-to-patient differences in capsule longevity best explain interpatient variability (Supplementary Fig. S6).

sec.title: Clinical evidence of immunologic pharmacodynamics
sec.p: To investigate the immune activity of AVB-001, peripheral blood from each patient was evaluated for changes in immune cell frequencies and fluctuations in protein biomarkers. Notably, flow cytometric analysis of peripheral immune cells demonstrated dose-dependent changes in circulating CD8+Ki67+, CD4+Ki67+, and NK+Ki67+ effector cells, consistent with IL2 activity (Fig. 3A–D). Across each cell population, the percent of cells peaked at day 8 after transplant and returned to baseline levels by day 14. Changes in frequency were not dose-dependent. Importantly, there was no notable increase in the percentage of CD4+ Tregs, which is a common disadvantage of systemic IL2 therapy.

Flow cytometric analysis of peak expression of surface immune checkpoint molecules (E) CTLA-4, (F) PD-1, and (G) TIM-3 on peripheral blood CD8+ and CD4+ T cells compared with baseline. Fold change over baseline of plasma concentration of (H) IFNγ, (I) IP-10, (J) CD25, (K) IL6, (L) TNFα, measured longitudinally, and (M) CA-125 on day 29 after capsule transplantation. sec.p: A well-documented phenomenon following immunotherapy is the upregulation of surface immune checkpoint receptors (e.g., PD-1, CTLA-4, TIM-3, LAG-3, and TIGIT) as a homeostatic mechanism to regulate immune activation and prevent excessive inflammation or autoimmunity (27). Further analysis of effector immune populations revealed a dose-dependent trend toward increased PD-1 and TIM-3 expression, particularly when considering maximum fold change. However, statistical significance was only observed for CTLA-4 expression (Fig. 3E–G). Although coexpression of multiple checkpoint receptors is often associated with T-cell exhaustion, the isolated upregulation of CTLA-4 has been reported as an early activation marker rather than a sign of functional decline (28–30).

Evaluation of serum biomarkers demonstrated robust immune activation, with dose-dependent increases observed in IFNγ, IP-10, CD25, and IL6 (Fig. 3H–K). Peak elevations of IFNγ and IL6 occurred at day 2 after treatment, whereas IP-10 and CD25 peaked at day 8. Whereas IFNγ, IP-10, and IL6 levels returned to baseline, CD25 remained elevated until day 30, particularly in dose levels 3 and 4, suggesting sustained immune activation at higher doses. TNFα levels also increased; however, the kinetics varied across dose cohorts, with dose levels 1 and 3 peaking at day 2, dose level 2 peaking at day 8, and dose level 4 peaking at day 5 (Fig. 3L). Finally, CA-125, a clinically relevant biomarker for ovarian cancer burden, exhibited an inverse correlation with AVB-001 dose. Higher AVB-001 doses were associated with attenuated increases in CA-125 by day 29, though this trend did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 3M).

Complete blood cell counts were evaluated for elevated eosinophils, platelets, and lymphocytes as secondary metrics for inflammatory response, coagulation activity, and immune activation, respectively. Increases were observed across all three cell types, though only eosinophils showed a marked elevation above the normal range, which is an expected effect of IL2 treatment (Supplementary Fig. S7A–S7C). This increase is consistent with IL2’s role in promoting eosinophil survival and expansion, likely driven by secondary cytokine signaling. Liver function was monitored via serum levels of AST, ALT, and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) over a 30-day period. Across all dose groups, transient increases were observed shortly after dosing. However, these elevations returned to baseline by days 15 to 20, and no sustained or dose-dependent hepatotoxicity was evident. These findings indicate that treatment was generally well tolerated from a hepatic standpoint, with only transient and reversible perturbations in liver enzymes at higher doses (Supplementary Fig. S7D).

These results, although demonstrating robust pharmacodynamic activity, indicate that the immunologic response to a single dose of AVB-001 is transient, with most immune biomarkers and effector cell populations returning to baseline within 2 weeks. This short duration of activity, although promising, underscores the potential need for repeated dosing to sustain immune engagement. Given the minimally invasive IP delivery method, the lack of observed antitherapy antibody formation in preclinical murine models, and the absence of Treg expansion seen clinically, we hypothesize that multiple doses of AVB-001 may prolong the proliferation and activation of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy. To investigate the safety and feasibility of a repeated-dosing regimen, we next evaluated AVB-001 readministration in NHPs.

sec.title: Pharmacology and safety following the second administration of AVB-001 in NHPs
sec.p: To evaluate the potential toxicity and safety of a second dose of AVB-001, NHPs were administered 10 μg/kg/day of AVB-001 hIL2 on day 0, followed by a second dose on day 28 via IP delivery using a laparoscopic technique (Fig. 4A). The study concluded 120 days after the first administration (Fig. 4B). Blood samples were collected at multiple time points, and physiologic parameters, including weight and body temperature, were monitored to assess the overall health of the animals.

sec.p: Serial blood collections were conducted on days 0, 1, 3, 7, 9, 14, 21, 28, 29, 31, 35, 37, 42, 49, and 56, biweekly thereafter, and on the day of termination. Serum concentrations of hIL2 were analyzed at each time point. As expected, hIL2 was undetectable in saline-treated animals. In AVB-001–treated animals, hIL2 was transiently detectable in the serum following each dose, with peak levels observed on day 1 after administration (mean IL2 levels on day 1: 7,134.5 ± 3,639.4 pg/mL; day 29: 7,583.5 ± 3,463.4 pg/mL). There were no significant differences in the kinetics of hIL2 secretion between the first and second administrations, with serum levels consistently returning to baseline within 7 to 14 days after dose (Fig. 4C).

To assess physiologic response to capsule administration and redosing, animal body weights and temperature were evaluated over the course of the study. No significant difference was evaluated when comparing AVB-001–treated primates with saline controls, indicating that the treatment was generally well tolerated (Fig. 4D).

Hematologic assessment revealed normal results across most measurements in vehicle-treated animals with a small number of occasions where leukocyte values (e.g., % lymphocytes, % neutrophils, or total white blood cells) were slightly out of range for only a single time point. However, these changes were transient, did not correlate with any other observations or findings, and are not of clinical concern (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. S8).

Liver function tests revealed only mild, transient AST and ALT elevations—some also present in controls—likely related to surgical procedures rather than treatment. GGT values stayed within healthy ranges (Fig. 4E). Kidney function parameters (creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and potassium) remained stable and within 20% of normal for the study’s duration, indicating no adverse renal effects (Fig. 4F).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This first-in-human phase I dose-escalation trial investigates the use of encapsulated protein producers to employ sustained and self-limited IP production of single-agent IL2 in patients with platinum-resistant HGSOC. At the evaluated doses, a single administration of AVB-001 resulted in a CBR of 14.3%. Fifty percent of patients experienced a period of SD with a median duration of clinical stability of 2.57 months. AVB-001 was found to be overall safe at the dose levels explored, though neither MTD nor RP2D was reached. One patient who received dose level 3 experienced a treatment-related bowel perforation that was managed surgically. Notably, at the time of surgical repair only 14 days after drug administration, previously observed diffuse carcinomatosis had resolved and significant peritoneal inflammation was noted. Furthermore, cytology obtained 1 month after the event was negative for malignant cells, with only inflammatory cells present. Following this event, dose level 3 was expanded to ensure safety prior to escalation to dose level 4. Given the overall favorable toxicity profile, these results suggest that additional dose-escalation is feasible to achieve a biologically and therapeutically effective dose.

The PK results support the potential for clinical activity of this agent even among a heavily pretreated cohort. After IP administration of the study agent, we observed a linear dose-dependent increase in plasma IL2 concentration when measured serially that peaked after 24 hours and subsequently declined to baseline levels by day 7. In addition to the expected increase in plasma IL2 levels after IP administration, further evidence of the biological activity of AVB-001 is demonstrated by immune system activation that persisted for approximately 2 weeks. Specifically, flow cytometric analysis revealed an increase in circulating CD4+, CD8+, and NK effector cell proliferation that was not accompanied by a concomitant increase in CD4+ Tregs. Consistent with these findings, clinical observations such as eosinophilia and rash likely reflect cytokine-driven immune activation and suggest a degree of controlled systemic immune activation following local IL2 release, rather than nonspecific toxicity. These findings are important because they suggest that, unlike systemically administered IL2, which has previously been associated with an increase in CD4+ Tregs that serve to suppress the potential immune response generated by the study agent, IP administration of AVB-001 selectively increases immune effector cells, which could perpetuate greater immune activation (21). Further evidence of the immunogenicity of this compound is exhibited by dose-dependent increases in IFNγ, IL10, CD25, and IL6. Taken together, these findings propose an immune-based mechanism that could provide meaningful clinical benefit in a subset of patients within this cohort at an effective dose.

As has been previously observed with the administration of IL2 immunotherapy, the administration of AVB-001 led to upregulation of surface immune checkpoint receptors (31). Immune checkpoint receptors (i.e., PD-1, CTLA-4, LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT) play a key role in the prevention of excessive immune activation. Within our study group, this phenomenon is observed via the dose-dependent upregulation of CTLA-4+ CD4 and CD8 T cells in peripheral blood. This upregulation suggests that combining AVB-001 with CTLA-4 antibody blockade may further potentiate the immunogenicity of the compound by limiting intrinsic suppressive checkpoint mechanisms. Checkpoint blockade has been widely studied across various cancer types, and at present, there are two anti–CTLA-4 antibodies available for clinical use (32, 33). Neither, however, is currently approved for use in ovarian cancer, and all approvals are for either single-agent administration or combination therapy with an anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 antibody. Combination anti–PD-1 checkpoint inhibition and intravenous IL2 therapy (nemvaleukin) demonstrated encouraging early results in the context of platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (PROC) as part of the phase I/II ARTISTRY-1 trial, which reported an ORR of 21% among 14 patients with PROC (34). These findings support the idea that, if able to reach a clinically active dose level and maintain safety, combination checkpoint inhibition and IL2 therapy could lead to meaningful clinical benefit in PROC and other tumor types that may present as secondary metastatic disease in the peritoneal cavity and benefit from both localized and systemic immune activation.

Building on the strong safety profile demonstrated in both human and prior NHP studies, the next phase of clinical development will focus on reinitiating the phase I trial at an increased IL2 dose and with repeat administration (13). In prior preclinical studies, migration or degradation of the encapsulated cell therapy was not observed following IP administration. Although these findings support the structural stability of AVB-001 in vivo, evaluation of capsule integrity, localization, and persistence will be incorporated into future clinical protocols to confirm translational relevance in humans. This escalation will aim to refine our understanding of AVB-001’s therapeutic window by identifying the MTD, any DLTs, and the RP2D. Additionally, an expansion of the phase I trial will incorporate repeated administration at the RP2D to better model long-term IL2 delivery and align more closely with the 16-week regimen used in Edwards and colleagues (22). However, unlike the prolonged, continuous IL2 infusions used in that study, AVB-001 represents a significantly improved delivery approach due to its novel constitutive IL2 production capabilities.

IP modeling data suggest that the highest dose of AVB-001 results in not only local IL2 levels comparable to the maximum tolerated dose in the 7-day infusion regimen evaluated by Edwards and colleagues (22) but also a more favorable safety profile. Additionally, preclinical studies in NHPs demonstrated that repeated administrations of AVB-001 at doses up to threefold higher than the highest dose evaluated in this first-in-human study were well tolerated. Although these findings are limited by small group sizes and known biologic differences between primates and humans, they support the hypothesis that higher IL2 exposures may be achievable with an acceptable safety profile. Importantly, these data motivate future clinical evaluation of dose-escalation, redosing, and combination strategies with targeted immunotherapies such as checkpoint inhibitors, which have historically been constrained by the toxicity of systemic and IP IL2 regimens (35, 36).

Although this study provides important insights into the clinical feasibility and therapeutic potential of AVB-001, several limitations should be addressed in future investigations. Although laparoscopic administration of AVB-001 enables localized IL2 delivery without the need for an indwelling catheter, reducing catheter-associated risks, this approach makes redosing or routine collection of ascites challenging due to the need to reaccess the peritoneal cavity. Given the potential for improved efficacy with a multidose regimen, future trials will include placement of an indwelling IP catheter to facilitate repeat administration and permit systematic collection of IP fluid and tumor biopsies, enabling a detailed evaluation of local tumor and peritoneal immune dynamics through immune cell characterization and immune signaling biomarker collection following AVB-001 administration. These insights will be critical for optimizing dosing strategies and informing potential combination therapies in subsequent trial phases. Although use of an indwelling catheter introduces risk of catheter-associated complications, as seen in investigations of IP IL12 and IL2, the sustained expression of IL2 by AVB-001 would minimize the required duration and result in a smaller number of necessary infusions than may otherwise be required (23, 37). Additionally, this strategy may improve scalability by eliminating the need for a laparoscopic procedure to administer the drug. In addition to the above limitations, it is important to note that the small sample size of the study which enrolled at a few academic centers may limit generalizability to the broader population (Supplementary Table S10).

To further enhance the clinical scalability of AVB-001, future efforts will also focus on optimizing the manufacturing process related to this allogeneic cell-based product. Increasing the per-cell production rate of hIL2 will reduce the number of cells and thus the volume of capsules per dose required to reach a target level of IL2 and enable cell expansion of multiple doses in parallel. Additionally, integrating high-throughput automated encapsulation to improve batch consistency will decrease the need for a technician to control voltage and enable efficient production of drug product at scale. These advancements will enable broad clinical availability, reduce production bottlenecks, and support the transition of AVB-001 from early-phase trials to larger, multicenter studies and ultimately commercialization. Together, these advancements will refine AVB-001’s clinical potential and accelerate its path toward broader therapeutic application.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that IP administration of AVB-001 is safe, feasible, and shows potential for meaningful clinical activity in a cohort of patients with platinum-resistant HGSOC. We found that peritoneal delivery of AVB-001 triggered a systemic immunogenic response, as evidenced by an increase in peripheral immune effector cells and inflammatory cytokines following administration. We further observed a dose-dependent upregulation of the CTLA-4 checkpoint on circulating CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, suggesting a role for combination therapies involving cytokines as priming agents to engage more effective checkpoint inhibition. Although efficacy was not observed at the current dose levels, these findings provide support investigation of higher or repeated dosing strategies.
